questions.question: Define the urban heat island and account for it using at least three causes, each with its mechanism.
questions.expected_answer: The urban heat island is the dome of warmer air over a city, with temperatures noticeably higher than the surrounding rural areas, peaking over the CBD, at night and in winter. Causes include: dark, low-albedo surfaces such as tar and concrete absorbing and storing radiation by day and releasing it at night; the lack of evaporation, since rain drains off sealed surfaces and vegetation is scarce, so solar energy heats surfaces instead of evaporating water; urban canyon geometry trapping radiation between walls and narrowing the night sky window through which streets cool; anthropogenic heat from vehicles, industry, heaters and bodies; and the haze blanket re-radiating escaping heat back down.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a pollution dome and a pollution plume, and why the dome over Highveld cities is worst on calm winter mornings.
questions.expected_answer: A pollution dome is the dome-shaped layer of polluted air that accumulates over a city under calm, stable conditions; when wind rises, the same pollution is stretched downwind as a pollution plume. The winter dome is worst because a temperature inversion seals the city: radiation cooling on clear calm nights puts cold air under warm, and the Kalahari High's subsiding air adds a persistent upper lid, so rising smoke loses buoyancy and spreads sideways. At the same time winter coal and wood burning for home heating increases the smoke supply, especially in townships, exactly when the lid sits lowest.

questions.question: Suggest reduction strategies for the urban heat island and the pollution dome, organising each strategy by the cause it attacks.
questions.expected_answer: Heat island: raise albedo with white or light roofs and pale paving; restore evaporation and shade with street trees, parks, green roofs, permeable paving and wetlands — the park dips in the temperature profile prove greening works; reduce anthropogenic heat through insulation, efficient buildings, public transport and cleaner energy; and design buildings to keep wind corridors open. Pollution dome: cut sources through household electrification, stack scrubbers and filters enforced under the Air Quality Act, vehicle emission standards, cleaner fuels and dust suppression; and work with the weather — no open burning on stable winter days, air-quality alerts during strong inversions, and industrial zoning downwind of dense settlement.
